dataset_family: Rumailah Hospital geriatric and memory clinic cohort, Hamad Medical Corporation / Weill Cornell Medicine-Qatar (Ponirakis/Malik corneal confocal microscopy programme), Doha, Qatar, recruited 2016-2020. 107 MCI analysed (33 progressed to dementia) plus 12 NCI controls at baseline only. No other corpus block reports this cohort.
method_family: Corneal confocal microscopy of the sub-basal corneal nerve plexus (Heidelberg HRT-3 with Rostock Cornea Module, topical anaesthesia, contact TomoCap; CNFD/CNBD/CNFL traced manually in CCMetrics). Compared head-to-head with 3T MRI volumetry (NeuroQuant). ROC/Youden cut-offs and multivariable logistic regression for MCI-to-dementia progression. Longitudinal clinic follow-up.
what_it_shows:
Ponirakis et al. 2023, Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology.
- Baseline corneal nerve fibre density, branch density and fibre length were lower in MCI (both later progressors and non-progressors) than in 12 NCI controls (p<=0.01-0.0001), and lower in the 33 MCI who progressed to dementia than in the 74 who did not.
- For progression, AUCs were 71-74% for the three main CCM measures against 78% for hippocampal and whole-brain volume. At Youden cut-offs, CCM accuracy was 72-75% against 68-69% for volumetry.
- After adjustment for age, MoCA and vascular covariates, abnormal CNFD (AOR 6.1) and CNBD (AOR 4.1) stayed associated with progression, while abnormal CNFL, hippocampal and whole-brain volume did not.
- The channel is corneal nerves, not retina or eye movements.
why:
PDF identity confirmed. The title 'Corneal nerve loss predicts dementia in patients with mild cognitive impairment', the author list (Ponirakis ... Malik) and DOI 10.1002/acn3.51747 match the block's full title, author list and DOI. The block header is only the file name. I read the whole extract (pp.1-9, up to the References).

STATED FORM, partly. The part it shows: an ocular imaging measure, taken at baseline, distinguishes MCI from no cognitive impairment and carries independent prognostic information for MCI-to-dementia progression, compared head-to-head with MRI volumetry in the study's own data. The channel is the corneal sub-basal nerve plexus. That is neither of the two ocular channels the Table A1 parenthesis names (retinal structure, eye-movement behaviour). It adds to neither named leg. It supports the statement only if the operator reads 'ocular channels' as open beyond the parenthesis. Under a strict reading of the parenthesis this is 'no'. That is a scope decision for the operator, not a design question.

Further limits, from the paper itself:
(a) The MCI-vs-NCI contrast rests on 12 controls recruited for baseline only (p.3). Diabetes was not excluded (p.2) and was present in about 51% of MCI. Controls' diabetes status is 'N/A', and their HbA1c was 5.7% against 7.1% and 6.7% in MCI (Table 1). Corneal nerve loss is a diabetic-neuropathy marker, so that contrast is potentially confounded. Within MCI, diabetes prevalence was equal in progressors and non-progressors (51.5% vs 51.4%), and Table S1 reports no CCM difference by diabetes (p.7). The prognostic comparison is therefore less exposed.
(b) 'Higher prognostic accuracy' refers to accuracy at Youden cut-offs. By AUC, volumetry was higher (78% vs 71-74%, Table 2).
(c) The text and Table 2 swap the CNBD and CNFL AUCs (73 vs 71).
(d) MCI was an ICD-10 clinical diagnosis without AD biomarkers, and 54 of 107 reverted to NCI (p.4, p.9).
(e) 'Scalable' is not tested. CCM here is a contact, anaesthetised, research-grade confocal examination with manual nerve tracing. The authors call for larger studies with automated analysis (p.9).

NARROWED FORM, partly. It fits 'preliminary, single-centre associations with MCI ... neither channel has been externally validated or shown to be scalable': single clinic, small control group, no external validation. But the narrowed wording lists only retinal imaging and saccadic measures. Admitting it would add a third ocular channel (corneal nerves), and the clause would need rewording to name it.

INDEPENDENCE. No shared sample, recruitment site or authors with P-5 (China), P-952 (Shenzhen), P-966 (GARD Korea) or P-105 (review). None with the other candidates either: P-255 (EU RECOGNISED), P-830 (a synthesis closed January 2021, before this 2023 study) and P-1152 (Morocco). It is a distinct dataset and method family.

Registry note: P-224's registry Modality 'Retinal imaging' is a miscode (the study is corneal), and study_design_type 'cross_sectional' is also wrong: it is a longitudinal cohort with 1-4.5 years of follow-up. Not a preprint: a peer-reviewed article in Ann Clin Transl Neurol. In the quotes, the extract's fi/fl ligatures and line-break hyphens are normalised, and '[±]' marks plus-minus signs the extract dropped.

quotes.quote: Of 107 participants with MCI aged 68.4 [±] 7.7 years, 33 (30.8%) progressed to dementia over 2.6-years of follow-up. Compared to participants with NCI (n = 12), participants who remained with MCI (n = 74) or progressed to dementia had lower corneal nerve measures (p < 0.0001). [± dropped by the extract]

However, CCM had a higher prognostic accuracy (72%–75% vs 68%–69%) for identifying individuals who progressed to dementia compared to hippocampus and whole brain volume. The adjusted odds ratio for progression to dementia was 6.1 (95% CI: 1.6–23.8) and 4.1 (95% CI: 1.2–14.2) higher with abnormal CCM measures, but was not significant for abnormal brain volume.

The area under the curve (AUC) to predict progression to dementia was 74% (95% CI 64–85%, p < 0.0001) for CNFD, 73% (95% CI 63%–84%, p < 0.0001) for CNBD, 71% (95% CI 61%–82%, p < 0.0001) for CNFL, 63% (95% CI 51%–74%, p < 0.05) for the CNBD/CNFD ratio, 78% (95% CI 67%–89%, p < 0.0001) for hippocampal volume, 78% (95% CI 66%–91%, p < 0.0001) for whole brain volume
Compared to participants with NCI, both progressors and non-progressors had significantly lower CNFD, CNBD, and CNFL (p ≤0.01–0.0001).

individuals with no cognitive impairment (NCI) and MCI aged 60–85 years were recruited from the geriatric and memory clinic in Rumailah Hospital, Qatar from 2016–2020 with a 1–4 year follow-up from 2017–2021. ... Diabetes was not excluded as it is highly prevalent in patients attending the clinic.
Twelve age-matched controls with no cognitive impairment (NCI) were recruited for baseline assessments only.

Table S1 shows that there were no differences in corneal confocal microscopy measures and volume of whole brain and hippocampi between participants with MCI with and without diabetes.

CCM analysis was performed in both eyes using the Heidelberg Retinal Tomograph 3 (HRT-3) device with the Rostock Cornea Module (RCM) (Heidelberg Engineering GmbH, Heidelberg, Germany). The cornea was locally anesthetized by instilling 1-drop of 0.4% benoxinate hydrochloride

We acknowledge the relatively small cohort size, short duration of follow up and the lack of more rigorous measures and biomarkers of AD, including cortical Ab-42 or tau PET, CSF Ab-42 or phosphorylated tau, CSF T-tau or FDG PET hypometabolism.
